An interesting quirk is that the largest model sometimes misidentifies elements with atomic numbers in the hundreds by their older, placeholder names. The FLOPs associated the corresponding dense layers (e.g. self-attention and dense feed-forward layers) are unchanged. ## Appendix B Definitions of linearity and breakthroughness Model performance on tasks exhibits a variety of behaviors across model scales. In this section we define metrics that we use to automatically categorize these behaviors along different axes. - • Linearity $L$ measures the extent to which performance improves reliably with scale. - • Breakthroughness $B$ measures to what extent a model is able to learn a task only once the model grows beyond a critical scale. Each metric is a function of a model’s performances $y_{i}$ at model scales $x_{i}$, sorted by model scale so that $x_{i}<x_{i+1}$. They are defined by $\displaystyle L$ $\displaystyle=\frac{I(y)}{\mathrm{RootMeanSquare}(\{y_{i+1}-y_{i}\}_{i})}\,,$ (1) $\displaystyle B$ $\displaystyle=\frac{I(y)}{\mathrm{RootMedianSquare}(\{y_{i+1}-y_{i}\}_{i})}\,,$ (2) where $I(y)=\mathrm{sign}({\rm argmax}_{i}y_{i}-{\rm argmin}_{i}y_{i})(\max_{i}y_{i}-\min_{i}y_{i})$ is a simple measure of the overall improvement in performance, $\mathrm{RootMeanSquare}(\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n})=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}z_{i}^{2}}$, and $\mathrm{RootMedianSquare}(\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n})=\sqrt{\mathrm{Median}(\{z_{i}^{2}\}_{i})}$.
Previous context: A research team wanted to automatically categorize how task performance changes across model scales, including whether a task shows a breakthrough, where performance jumps only once a model passes a critical size. They had scores at a series of model sizes per task, some of which are noisy or contain isolated large jumps between adjacent scales. They already had a linearity measure based on overall improvement divided by the typical size of step-to-step changes.
Previous question: How should the team define a breakthrough measure that is robust to noisy or outlier score changes between scales?

Problem: Which experimental setting to use to test latent two-hop reasoning, given that prior evidence was mixed and confounded
Write-up text before the decision: # Lessons from Studying Two-Hop Latent Reasoning arXiv:2411.16353. cs.CL, cs.AI. Submitted 2024-11-25. Latest version v4, 2025-11-23. ## Authors Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak, Owain Evans ## Details - License: http://arxiv.org/licenses/nonexclusive-distrib/1.0/ ## Versions - v1: 2024-11-25 - v2: 2025-01-06 - v3: 2025-09-06 - v4: 2025-11-23 --- Full text of v4. ## Abstract Large language models can use chain-of-thought (CoT) to externalize reasoning, potentially enabling oversight of capable LLM agents. Prior work has shown that models struggle at two-hop question-answering without CoT. This capability is so basic that if it was a fundamental limitation, it would imply that many complex agentic tasks would similarly require CoT. We investigate LLM latent reasoning capabilities using two-hop question answering as a case study. Previous work on the gap between latent and externalized two-hop reasoning produced mixed evidence with inconclusive results.
Previous context: A research team wants to know whether language models can perform two-hop reasoning (composing two separate facts) internally without writing out chain-of-thought, which matters for whether chain-of-thought can be relied on for oversight. Prior work on the gap between latent and externalized two-hop reasoning gave mixed, inconclusive evidence, with results confounded by factors such as what the models saw in pretraining. The team must choose an experimental setting to test this capability more cleanly.
Previous question: Which experimental setting should the team use to test latent two-hop reasoning given the mixed and confounded prior evidence?
